questions.question: For $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and an index set $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$, what is the principal submatrix $[A]_I$?
options: The rows indexed by $I$, with all columns kept
What is left after deleting the rows and columns in $I$
The rows in $I$ together with the columns not in $I$
The rows and the columns indexed by the same set $I$

questions.question: Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, and let $A_k$ contain its first $k$ rows and columns. When is $A$ positive definite according to Sylvester's criterion?
options: Exactly when $\det(A_k)>0$ for $k=1,\dots,n$
Exactly when the full determinant $\det A$ is positive
Exactly when every diagonal entry of $A$ is positive
Exactly when $(-1)^k\det(A_k)>0$ for $k=1,\dots,n$

questions.question: A real symmetric $3\times3$ matrix has leading principal minors $-2$, $3$ and $4$, in increasing order of size. Which conclusion follows?
options: It is negative definite because the first minor is negative
It is positive definite because the last two minors are positive
It is neither positive definite nor negative definite
It is negative definite because the first two signs alternate

questions.question: Which conditions on $b$ and $c$ are necessary and sufficient for the real symmetric matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ to be positive semidefinite?
options: $c\ge0$, with no restriction on $b$
$b=0$ and $c\ge0$
$b\ge0$ and $c\ge0$
Only that $c$ vanishes, with $b$ arbitrary

questions.question: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has positive leading principal minors. Why does this not establish that $x^\top Ax>0$ for every nonzero real $x$?
options: The criterion also requires every entry to be positive
The criterion requires all principal minors, even for definiteness
The criterion requires positive off-diagonal products
The criterion requires symmetry, which $A$ lacks

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$, what does Sylvester's criterion give?
options: Indefinite
Negative definite
Positive definite
Positive semidefinite, but not positive definite

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is the third leading minor $\det(A_3)$?
For which values of $a$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&a\end{pmatrix}$ positive definite?
Counting principal minors by their nonempty index sets, how many does a $3\times3$ matrix have, and how many of them are leading?
options: $9$ principal, $3$ leading
$7$ principal, $3$ leading
$3$ principal, all leading
$8$ principal, $3$ leading

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, what do the principal minors show?
options: Positive semidefinite only
Positive definite, because $\det(A_1)=1>0$
Indefinite, because $\det A=0$
Negative semidefinite, because $\det A=0$

questions.question: A real symmetric matrix $A$ has a zero leading principal minor. What does Sylvester's criterion still decide from this information?
options: That $A$ is positive definite if the other minors are positive
That $A$ is indefinite, because a leading minor vanishes
Only that $A$ is not definite
Nothing, since the criterion no longer applies to $A$

questions.question: Let $A$ be a real symmetric matrix. Relabelling its variables replaces $A$ by $PAP^\top$, where $P$ is a permutation matrix. What happens to Sylvester's test?
options: The leading minors and the conclusion both stay the same
The leading minors may change, the conclusion does not
The conclusion may change, as definiteness depends on order
The test can no longer be applied to the new matrix

questions.question: What can be concluded about a symmetric $2\times2$ matrix $A$ with $\det A<0$?
options: $A$ is negative definite
$A$ is negative semidefinite
Nothing without the sign of $a_{11}$
$A$ is indefinite

questions.question: At a critical point $a$ of a $C^2$ function, $H_f(a)=\begin{pmatrix}-4&2\\2&-3\end{pmatrix}$. What does Sylvester's criterion show?
options: Negative definite, so $a$ is a strict local maximum
Positive definite, as $\det H_f(a)=8>0$
Indefinite, as the entries have mixed signs
Negative definite, so $a$ is a strict local minimum

questions.question: Classify $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&0\\1&-2&0\\0&0&-3\end{pmatrix}$ by its leading principal minors.
options: Positive definite
Indefinite
Negative definite
Negative semidefinite, but not definite

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&1&2\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$ all leading principal minors are zero. Is $A$ positive semidefinite?
options: Yes: its leading principal minors are nonnegative
Yes: its diagonal entries are nonnegative
It cannot be decided from minors at all
No: a non-leading principal minor is negative

questions.question: For a real symmetric $3\times3$ matrix, every principal minor of odd order is nonpositive and every leading principal minor of even order is nonnegative. Do these conditions guarantee negative semidefiniteness?
options: Yes: the alternating weak sign conditions suffice
No: a non-leading minor of order two may be negative
Yes: checking every odd-order minor closes the gap
No: negative semidefiniteness requires a negative determinant

questions.question: Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, let $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be nonempty, and let $B=[A]_I$ keep the rows and columns indexed by $I$. Which argument proves $\det B>0$?
options: Extend each nonzero vector for $B$ by zeros; positivity for $A$ then makes $B$ positive definite
Use $\det A>0$; determinants of principal submatrices must have the same sign
Use the positive diagonal of $B$; positive diagonal entries make $B$ positive definite
Permute $B$ into the leading block; its determinant must then equal an original leading minor

questions.question: For which $a$ is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&0\\a&1&a\\0&a&1\end{pmatrix}$ positive definite?
options: $a<\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$
$|a|<\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$
$|a|<\tfrac12$

questions.question: Is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&5\end{pmatrix}$ positive semidefinite?
options: No: its full determinant is zero
Yes: all its principal minors are nonnegative
No: its principal minor indexed by $\{1,3\}$ is negative
Yes: it is also positive definite
